title: Choosing honest work
hookLine: kirat karni means work that harms no one and is done honestly
tomorrow: the stall's scale reads a little heavy. does Simran say so?

lines: MORE THAN A WHOLE MORNING'S PAY.
cards: Saturday, early, and Simran is stacking peaches into a pyramid at a farmers' market stall. Her first real job. Her phone buzzes.

It's Dev from her class: easy money. His cousin's shop pays for every five-star review, and you don't even have to go there. Twenty reviews, he writes, and that's more than you'll make all morning, from your couch.
Simran looks at her pyramid. Then at the line of people already waiting for the stall to open.

teach.b: Sikhs have a name for what Simran is weighing: kirat karni, earning a living honestly. It sits beside two others in the Sikh life: naam japna, remembering the Name, and vand chhakna, sharing what you have.
And there's a story Sikhs tell about it. Tradition says Guru Nanak, on his travels, stayed with Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned his bread with his hands.
A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a great feast and was offended that the Guru didn't come.
When Nanak did come, the story goes, he took Lalo's plain bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezed. From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's came blood.
The difference wasn't the menu. It was how the money behind it was made. The Granth says the same thing without the drama.
On ang 1245, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: one who eats what he earns by his own work, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path. So clean work isn't about how fancy the job is.
It's honest, and it harms no one.
Dev's reviews harm every stranger who trusts them. Simran's peaches harm nobody. She types back: no thanks, i'm at the stall.
Then she opens the stall to the line.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, alongside naam japna and vand chhakna; the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago is told in Sikh homes and gurdwaras.

o: earning a living honestly, by work that harms no one
working only for the gurdwara, never for pay
picking whichever job pays the most per hour

games.q: who's who in honest work — tap the pairs.
p: a carpenter who earned with his hands
a rich official with a great feast
earn by your work, give some away

s: kirat karni means only manual labor counts as honest
it's about honesty and harm, not how fancy the job is.
in the story, Lalo's plain bread gave milk
tradition says Bhago's rich food gave blood: the difference was how it was earned.
easy money is clean if no one ever finds out how it was made
clean work is honest and harms no one, seen or unseen.

games.q: a classmate's side hustle pays well: selling 'guaranteed' answers to next week's test. going by today, what's the question to ask?
o: does it harm anyone who trusts it? then it isn't clean work.
is it against the law? if not, it's fine.
does it pay more than a normal job? then why not.
games.why: kirat karni is work that's honest and harms no one. Lalo's bread over Bhago's feast: what matters is how it's earned.

practice: Look at your own hands for the whole sit: the palms, the knuckles, whatever marks your work has left. Bring to mind one honest thing they made, fixed or carried this week, however small, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Choosing honest work. Kirat karni: earning a living honestly, by work that harms no one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work.

carryVoice: Your line: clean work. Lalo's plain bread, earned honestly, not Bhago's rich feast. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 1245 (Sarang ki Var, Guru Nanak: ghaal khaae kichh hathahu dei, nanak raahu pachhaanahi sei), paraphrased
Janamsakhi tradition: Guru Nanak with Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago at Saidpur, told as a story
